overview: A two-page Department of State “List of Papers,” compiled on October 1, 1945, indexing documents in file 894.642 on Japanese marine engineering and shipbuilding. The entries, covering 1941 through approximately 1944, concern Japan’s merchant-ship construction program, the halted construction of the SS Kasuga Maru, wartime wooden-vessel production and requisitioning, shipbuilding at Chinese-owned Hong Kong yards, tanker construction at Dalian, and orders for Mitsubishi-built freighters. The listed sources include the Justice Department, the U.S. Maritime Commission, the Department of State’s Far Eastern affairs staff, diplomatic posts in Switzerland and China, and translated German press reports.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on Japanese marine engineering and shipbuilding
subfiles.about: An index to papers concerning Japan’s shipbuilding industry, merchant-vessel program, and wartime shipping measures.
subfiles.summary: The list describes numbered papers 40 through 50, dating from 1941 to approximately 1944, drawn from U.S. agencies, diplomatic posts, and German press reporting. Subjects include the suspension of work on the SS Kasuga Maru, wooden-vessel construction in Hong Kong and Japan, the requisitioning of motor sailing ships, tanker construction at Dalian, and an order for seven Mitsubishi-built freighters. It also records correspondence involving reports by Leland Harrison and Roy M. Melbourne, photographs of Japanese wooden ships and military orders, and a reported statement by Marine Minister Shimada on shipbuilding progress.

interest: This index is useful as a compact map of American wartime intelligence about Japanese commercial and military-related shipbuilding. It shows how information was assembled from diplomatic telegrams, interagency correspondence, photographs, enemy press translations, and reporting from occupied Asian ports. Particularly notable are the references to rapid wooden-ship construction, the requisitioning of motor sailing vessels, Japanese-directed work in Hong Kong, and major tanker and freighter projects—evidence of attempts to compensate for wartime shipping shortages and losses.
